Model card

Everything we did, and everything we know is wrong with it

A model card is the document that lets someone else decide whether to believe you. This one lists every equation, every input, every assumption and every known error. If a number in the app is not derivable from this page, that is a bug.

1. What the model claims, and what it does not

Field Shift answers one question: in how many of the last 33 years would this rotation's irrigation requirement have fitted inside the water this farmer can supply? That is the reliability number. It is a count, not a score.

It does not claim to predict yield, income or adoption. Gross margins are editable regional defaults expressed as a P10/P50/P90 band, and they are used only to rank rotations against each other — never to promise a farmer money.

The design rule. A number that cannot be wrong is not worth showing. Reliability can be wrong: it names specific years, and those years can be checked against the rainfall and soil-moisture record. That is why it is the headline instead of a weighted score out of 100.

2. Data sources

SourceVariableResolutionTag
NASA POWERT2M, T2M_MAX, T2M_MIN, PRECTOTCORR, RH2M, WS2M, ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN, GWETROOT0.5° × 0.64°, daily, 1991–2024reanalysis

IPCC AR6 AtlasSSP2-4.5 South Asia delta: +1.9 °C, −6% precipitationregional meansimulated

POWER is a reanalysis product (MERRA-2), not a satellite retrieval. We tag it reanalysis everywhere it appears, including in the app, because calling it "NASA satellite data" would be false.

What NDVI is and is not used for. MOD13Q1 is read through the Planetary Computer COG mirror of the NASA LP DAAC product, 3×3 pixel mean around the field coordinate. It feeds the Field Memory strip and the NDVI prediction in the ledger. It does not enter the water balance, the nitrogen balance or the search — those run on POWER and SoilGrids alone. If a bundle has no composite yet, the app says so and withholds the NDVI prediction rather than substituting a plausible number. The map layer is a live NASA GIBS tile service and is independent of the bundle.

Soil is sampled, not assumed. The point-query API returns null when the exact 250 m pixel is masked — water, built-up land, or a gap in the grid — and the Sheikhupura coordinate is one of those. So the pipeline reads the same grid through the SoilGrids WCS endpoint, which serves a small GeoTIFF per property, and takes the median of the valid pixels within 2.2 km of the field point. That is a better statistic than a single pixel: it is a neighbourhood, and the bundle records how many pixels went into each value. Every field in the app carries a real SoilGrids texture — Sheikhupura comes back a silt loam at 22% clay, 22% sand, 56% silt, which is what the Punjab canal-command literature describes. None of the five fields falls back to a hand-written regional default.

Known bias. MERRA-2 underestimates monsoon rainfall over the Punjab. The Sheikhupura record averages 477 mm/yr against a station climatology nearer 600 mm. We use it anyway because it is consistent across the whole 34-year record, and we note that the bias makes the irrigation requirement an upper bound — the model asks for more water than the field probably needs. That direction is the safe one for a farmer deciding whether to switch.

3. Reference evapotranspiration

FAO-56 Penman-Monteith, computed daily from the POWER record.

ET₀ = [0.408 Δ (Rₙ − G) + γ (900/(T+273)) u₂ (eₛ − eₐ)] / [Δ + γ (1 + 0.34 u₂)] Δ slope of the saturation vapour curve γ psychrometric constant Rₙ net radiation from ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN u₂ wind at 2 m eₛ − eₐ vapour pressure deficit from RH2M and T2M

ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN arrives in MJ/m²/day and is used as-is. It is not multiplied by 3.6 — that conversion applies to kW·h/m²/day, and getting it wrong inflates ET₀ by a factor of 3.6. We checked the response header rather than assuming.

For the Sheikhupura field this gives a mean ET₀ of 1,769 mm/yr (4.84 mm/day), which is consistent with published Punjab values.

4. Crop water requirement

Single crop coefficient approach, FAO-56 Chapter 8, with a daily soil-water balance.

ETc = Kc × ET₀ Kc = Kcb + Ke basal + soil evaporation Kcb = Kcb,ini → Kcb,mid → Kcb,end over four growth stages TAW = 1000 (θFC − θWP) Zr total available water, mm RAW = p × TAW readily available water Ks = (TAW − Dr) / (TAW − RAW) water stress coefficient, 0 to 1 Dr,t = Dr,t−1 − (Pe + I) + ETc,t daily depletion IRreq = Σ max(0, ETc,t − Pe,t − ΔDr) irrigation requirement

p is the FAO-56 depletion fraction per crop, adjusted for ETc. Rooting depth Zr grows through the season. Twenty crops are parameterised in engine/crops.js, each with its Kcb curve, stage lengths, rooting depth, depletion fraction, heat threshold and nitrogen fixation rate.

Effective rainfall

USDA-SCS monthly relationship, applied to monthly totals and distributed back to days in proportion to daily rainfall so that timing is preserved.

Pe = P (125 − 0.2 P) / 125 for P < 250 mm Pe = 125 + 0.1 P for P ≥ 250 mm

Soil hydraulics

Saxton & Rawls (2006) pedotransfer functions, from SoilGrids texture and organic carbon.

θ1500 = −0.024 A + 0.487 C + 0.006 M + 0.005 (S·A) − 0.013 (C·M) + 0.068 (A·M) + 0.031 θ33 = −0.251 S + 0.195 C + 0.011 M + 0.006 (S·A) − 0.027 (C·M) + 0.452 (A·M) + 0.299 AWC = θ33 − θ1500 available water capacity, m/m S sand %, C clay %, M organic matter %, A = 100 − S − C

When SoilGrids is unreachable the pipeline falls back to a documented regional default and says so in the app, on the field profile, in the source list. It does not silently substitute.

5. Reliability, defined exactly

requirement(y) = IRreq(kharif, y) + IRreq(rabi, y) unmet(y) = max(0, requirement(y) − supply) reliable(y) = 1 if unmet(y) ≤ tolerance, else 0 reliability = Σ reliable(y) / N

supply is the water the farmer says they can deliver in a year, in mm over the field. tolerance defaults to 0 mm. N is the number of years with a complete pair of seasons for every crop in the region pack — 33 for Punjab, 1991–2023.

Heat is reported separately, never folded in. A rotation can be water-reliable and heat-exposed at the same time, and collapsing those into one index would hide the thing the farmer most needs to know. Heat days count days above the crop's critical maximum during its heat-sensitive window.

Worked example, Punjab field, 900 mm supply. Rice–wheat requires 938 mm on average and fits inside the budget in 13 of 33 years — 39% reliable, 20 failing years. Cotton–chickpea requires 703 mm and fits in 28 of 33 — 85% reliable. Both numbers are reproducible from the shipped data with npm test.

6. Soil loss

RUSLE, with a cover factor driven by the simulated canopy and residue cover.

A = R · K · LS · C · P R modified Fournier index, monthly (Renard & Freimund 1994) K Williams (1995) erodibility from texture and organic carbon LS Wischmeier & Smith slope-length factor from slope % C cover factor from mean canopy cover and residue retention P support practice: none 1.0, contour 0.5, terrace 0.25

7. Nitrogen and soil carbon

A four-season nitrogen balance: fixation by legumes, removal by grain and residue, leaching and volatilisation losses as fixed fractions. Soil organic carbon follows a 20-year first-order trajectory toward a residue-dependent equilibrium.

N_net = Σ (fixation − removal − losses) / 4 seasons dSOC/dt = k (SOC_eq − SOC) k = 0.02 /yr, SOC_eq from residue input

These are the weakest numbers in the model. They are directionally right and they rank rotations sensibly, but they are not calibrated against measured trials. We show them because a rotation that mines nitrogen is a real risk, and hiding that would be worse than approximating it.

8. The search

Every legal four-season sequence in a region pack is enumerated and evaluated against the whole record. For Punjab that is 8 kharif × 6 rabi × 8 kharif × 6 rabi = 2,304 sequences. Many are the same two-year cycle started at a different point, so results are de-duplicated by canonical rotation, leaving 1,176 distinct cycles and 152,064 simulated seasons.

The efficient frontier is the Pareto set over four objectives: maximise reliability, maximise nitrogen balance, minimise soil loss, maximise downside margin. Nothing on the frontier is beaten by anything else on all four at once.

The recommendation rule is stated, not hidden. We prefer a rotation that beats current practice on margin, nitrogen and reliability simultaneously. If none does, we fall back to the most reliable option and say that we did. On the Punjab field, no rotation is both 100% reliable and as profitable as rice–wheat, so the recommendation is 85% reliable and more profitable — and the app says exactly that.

9. The 2050 stress test

A uniform delta of +1.9 °C and −6% precipitation is applied to every day of the observed record, and the whole search is re-run. The deltas come from the IPCC AR6 Atlas for SSP2-4.5 in South Asia.

This is a sensitivity test, not a forecast. It does not model CO₂ fertilisation, changed rainfall intensity, or adaptation. It answers one narrow question: if the mean climate moved this far, which rotations would still fit inside the same water supply? Tagged simulated.

10. What we know is wrong

  • Rainfall is biased low. MERRA-2 under-reports monsoon totals in the Punjab. The irrigation requirement is therefore an upper bound.
  • Gross margins are regional defaults, not this farm's books. They are a P10/P50/P90 band precisely because a point estimate would be a lie. Every margin number in the app is editable.
  • Nitrogen and SOC are uncalibrated. Directionally correct, quantitatively approximate.
  • The field is a demonstration polygon. 2.4 ha drawn around a coordinate, not a surveyed boundary. The soil, climate and NDVI are real for that coordinate; the boundary is not.
  • No pest or disease dynamics. We count family breaks as a proxy for rotation benefit. We do not model pathogen populations.
  • No irrigation efficiency. Supply is treated as water delivered to the root zone. Canal conveyance losses, which are large in Punjab, are not modelled.
  • One climate delta, one scenario. No ensemble, no uncertainty band on the 2050 result.
  • Validation is directional. The failure flags line up with the driest years and with lower reanalysis root-zone wetness. That is a consistency check on a reanalysis product, not an independent satellite validation.

11. What would make us abandon this

If the failure flags did not line up with observed dry years, the model would be noise and we would say so. On the Punjab field, all five of the driest years in the record are flagged as failures for rice–wheat, and years the model passes are 0.06 m³/m³ wetter in the reanalysis root-zone record than years it fails. That is a weak signal in absolute terms and we present it as such — but it points the right way, and it is checkable by anyone with the same data.

12. The ten questions the brief asks you to understand

The challenge guide ends with ten questions a team is expected to be able to answer. We answer them here rather than in a slide, because a judge should be able to check each one against the model rather than take our word for it.

1 · What is crop rotation, and why does it matter for soil health?

Growing different crops in a planned sequence on the same ground. It matters because a monoculture mines the same nutrients from the same depth, hosts the same pathogens, and leaves the soil bare in the same months every year. Rotation breaks all three cycles at once. In this model the three effects are separate and separately visible: nitrogen balance (§7), soil loss (§6), and family-break intervals for disease (§4).

2 · How do changing temperature and rainfall affect production?

Temperature sets demand, rainfall sets supply, and the gap is irrigation. A warmer year raises ET₀, which raises the crop water requirement for the same yield. A drier year lowers effective rainfall. Either one widens the gap. Field Shift does not model yield directly — it models whether the gap can be closed with the water the farmer actually has, year by year, which is why the headline is a failure rate rather than a tonnage.

3 · How can satellite data help monitor soil moisture and vegetation health?

Soil moisture is measured directly by SMAP's L-band radiometer (root-zone product on the map) and inferred from the MERRA-2 land surface model in the POWER record we run the balance on. Vegetation health comes from MODIS NDVI, which is a 16-day composite of the normalised difference between near-infrared and red reflectance — green, photosynthesising canopy reads high, bare or stressed ground reads low. We use NDVI as corroboration, not as an input: it tells you the crop grew, not how much water it needed.

4 · What is the difference between Landsat, SMAP, GPM and ECOSTRESS?

They answer different questions at different scales, and the honest answer to "why not use all of them" is that a 33-year daily water balance needs a consistent daily series, which none of them provides on its own.

MissionResolutionRevisitMeasuresRole here
Landsat 8/930 m optical, 100 m thermal16 days Surface reflectance, land surface temperature Not in the bundle. 30 m is finer than a 2.4 ha field needs, and a 16-day repeat can miss the monsoon break that decides the season. MODIS gives daily coverage at 250 m, which is the right trade for a field-scale balance.
SMAP9–36 km2–3 days Surface and root-zone soil moisture Live map layer (L4 root zone). Not in the balance: 9 km is coarser than the field, and the record starts in 2015 — too short for a 33-year failure rate.
GPM IMERG0.1°30 minutes Precipitation rate Live map layer. Not in the balance: IMERG starts in 2000, which would cut the sample from 33 years to 24 and change what the failure rate means.
ECOSTRESS38 × 69 mIrregular, target-requested Evapotranspiration, land surface temperature Not used. The revisit is not systematic, so a monthly composite would mosaic different days. A daily water balance cannot be built on it.
GRACE-FO~300 km masconsMonthly Total water storage anomaly Live map layer, used qualitatively. It is the evidence that the aquifer trend makes the current rotation untenable — not a term in the equation.
MODIS250 m – 1 kmDaily NDVI, land surface temperature NDVI in the bundle (MOD13Q1); LST as a live layer.
MERRA-2 via POWER0.5° × 0.625°Daily Temperature, rain, humidity, wind, radiation, root-zone wetness The backbone. Reanalysis, not a satellite retrieval, and tagged as such everywhere.

5 · How can a farmer identify crops suited to their soil and climate?

By testing candidates against the actual record rather than a suitability chart. Every crop in the library carries stage lengths, basal crop coefficients, rooting depth and depletion fraction from FAO-56; the soil supplies field capacity and wilting point from texture; the climate supplies 33 years of demand and rainfall. A crop that cannot close its water gap in most years is not suited, whatever a zone map says.

6 · How do nitrogen-fixing crops improve fertility?

Legumes symbiotically fix atmospheric N₂ into plant-available forms, so a legume in the rotation adds nitrogen instead of removing it. In the model each crop carries an nfix term; chickpea and lentil are net positive, cereals are strongly negative. This is why the recommended Punjab rotation gains nitrogen where rice–wheat loses it — and why the app shows both numbers side by side rather than a single score.

7 · How do cover crops reduce erosion and retain moisture?

Ground cover intercepts raindrop energy and slows surface flow, which is the C factor in RUSLE; roots and residue improve infiltration, which is the moisture half. Field Shift models the cover term explicitly and lets the farmer toggle residue retention, because burning is the single largest lever on soil loss in the Punjab and it is a decision the farmer actually makes. The app shows the soil-loss difference between retaining and burning rather than asserting that residue is good.

8 · How does rotation interrupt pest and disease cycles?

Pathogens and pests are usually host-specific: they overwinter in residue or soil and need the same host family back within a season or two to persist. A break of two or more seasons to an unrelated family starves them out. We model this as a family-break count per rotation and report it as a count, not a probability — we do not simulate pathogen populations, and §10 says so.

9 · How are satellite observations combined with local soil measurements?

The satellite record supplies the daily forcing — temperature, humidity, wind, radiation and rainfall from POWER, NDVI from MODIS. The local half supplies the soil: clay, sand, silt, organic carbon, pH and bulk density from SoilGrids at 250 m, which convert through Saxton & Rawls into field capacity, wilting point and available water capacity. The two meet in the daily soil-water balance: climate sets demand, soil sets how much of the supply the root zone can actually hold. Neither half is sufficient alone, which is the point of the brief.

10 · How does a decision-support tool compare at least three strategies?

By scoring all of them on the same years with the same soil and the same water supply, and then refusing to collapse the result into one number. Field Shift compares seven rotations side by side — the farmer's current practice plus six alternatives — on reliability, mean irrigation requirement, nitrogen balance, soil loss and the P10 margin. Where two options trade off against each other, the app says so instead of hiding it behind a weighted score. The recommendation rule is stated in §5 and in the app itself.
